sections.h2: Selling a house in Queen Creek, AZ
sections.html:
A Queen Creek homeowner has three ways to sell: hire an agent, go without one, or take a cash buyer's offer, which needs no mortgage behind it. This is a town of owners, with 90.2 percent of occupied homes lived in by the people who own them.

  • Agent listing: wide marketing for the house, while you manage showings, repair requests from the buyer's inspection and the lender's approval timeline.
  • Selling alone: you pick the price, talk to buyers yourself and prepare the deed along with the affidavit of property value.
  • Cash sale: no lender is involved, so weigh the offer against what a listing would leave you after fees and repairs.

If an association governs your street, ask it for its governing documents and any unpaid dues before you accept an offer. A buyer will want them at closing.

About 89,770 people lived in Queen Creek as of July 1, 2025, a 51.4 percent jump over the 2020 base. Over 2020 to 2024, a median owner-occupied home was worth $635,400, rent ran $2,210 and household income reached $141,978. Households average 3.21 people and 30.5 percent of residents are under 18, which points to families as your likely buyers.

Commutes average 31.1 minutes, so buyers will ask about drive times to work and to the freeway. Know your answers before the first showing, and have them ready for your title company too, since the buyer's lender will often ask the same questions, whether the buyer is local or relocating.

Most of Queen Creek is in Maricopa County. The eastern and southern edges reach into Pinal County, and the Ironwood Crossing neighborhood joined the town by annexation in 2018. Your parcel number tells you which county records the deed and which assessor handles the parcel.

Sun does most of the damage to a house in this town. About 103 days a year reach 100 degrees, 11 of them hit 110 or higher, and the record is 119 degrees. Only about 8.3 inches of rain falls in a year, mostly in the July to mid-September monsoon. Buyers look at:

  • Air conditioning: the age of the unit and its service history
  • Roof and attic: sustained heat ages roofing materials, and attic ventilation matters
  • Pool equipment, if there is a pool: pumps and decking see heavy use in long summers
  • Grading and gutters: a short, hard monsoon storm can pool water against a foundation

Hard freezes of 28 degrees or lower come only every couple of years, so frozen pipes worry buyers less than in northern Arizona.

sections.h2: Which school district serves the address?
sections.html: The town is covered by six public school districts. Queen Creek Unified holds most of the Maricopa County side, along with parts of Higley Unified and Chandler Unified. Over in Pinal County the districts are Florence Unified, J. O. Combs Unified and Apache Junction Unified. District lines ignore town limits, so a buyer should confirm the school for the exact address.

Short-term renting is possible in Queen Creek if the owner registers the property with the town. A.R.S. 9-500.39 lets every municipality's residents rent short term, and Queen Creek has removed its license and fees while keeping registration. Before registering, an owner needs to:

  • Confirm the property lies inside the town limits, using the town's "Do I live in QC?" map.
  • Get a transaction privilege tax license from the Arizona Department of Revenue, which applies even when the owner books through an online marketplace.
  • Register the rental with the Maricopa County Assessor (602-506-3406) or Pinal County Assessor (520-866-6361) under A.R.S. 33-1902.
  • Provide the parcel number and emergency contact information.

Send registration questions to Development@QueenCreekAZ.gov. HOA rules can be stricter than the town's, so a buyer should read them before counting on rental income.

sections.h2: How the county line affects your paperwork
sections.html:
The county line affects more than recording. Property tax bills, assessor records and any short-term rental registration all follow the county. If you are unsure, look at the parcel number on your latest tax bill and call the matching assessor before you list.

The Ironwood Crossing neighborhood joined the town only in 2018, so older paperwork for a home there may carry an address or jurisdiction that no longer matches. Ask the title company to check that the legal description and the town and county names agree, since a mismatch can delay recording. Catching it early costs a phone call. Catching it on closing day can cost a week.

Permits, zoning, engineering, traffic applications and code complaints all run through the town's Development Nexus portal. Search a property's project history there, or call 480-358-3003 for help. Real payment emails come only from DevSvcsNexus@queencreekaz.gov. Fees are paid in the portal by ACH or credit card, and the town never requests a wire transfer.

If you built an addition, patio cover or pool, check the portal for permit records before you list. A missing final inspection is better fixed by you than discovered by a buyer's inspector.

Maricopa County charges a standard $30 to record a document, and a certified copy runs $1 a page plus $3 for certification. On the Pinal County side, call that county's recorder for the current fee.

A.R.S. 11-1133 puts an affidavit on every deed that changes ownership, signed by buyer and seller or their agents. It states the price, the parcel number and whether an owner or a tenant will live there. Without a complete affidavit or an exemption notation, the recorder rejects the deed. Title or escrow normally drafts it alongside the deed.

1. Find your parcel number and confirm the county.
  2. Check the Development Nexus portal for permit records, and fix any missing final inspection.
  3. Collect HOA documents and any unpaid dues statement.
  4. Gather written offers and compare your net from each.
  5. Open escrow so the title company prepares the deed and affidavit.
  6. The deed is recorded in the right county and you receive your proceeds.

A cash buyer skips the lender's timeline. The HOA, permit and recording steps still apply, and they set the real pace of your closing.

faqs.q: Is Queen Creek in Maricopa County or Pinal County?
faqs.a: Both. Most of the town is in Maricopa County, and the eastern and southern edges reach into Pinal County. Your parcel number shows which county recorder and assessor apply.

faqs.q: Does Queen Creek require short-term rental registration?
faqs.a: Yes. The town dropped its rental license and fees, but owners still register the property. You need a transaction privilege tax license, the parcel number and an emergency contact. Email Development@QueenCreekAZ.gov with questions.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Maricopa County?
faqs.a: The standard fee is $30 per document. A copy costs $1 per page, and certification adds $3 per document. A deed needs the affidavit of property value.

faqs.q: How many people live in Queen Creek?
faqs.a: An estimated 89,770 as of July 1, 2025, up from 59,519 in the 2020 census and 26,361 in 2010.

faqs.q: Which school district serves my Queen Creek address?
faqs.a: It depends on the address. Most of the Maricopa County part is in Queen Creek Unified, with some areas in Higley Unified and Chandler Unified. The Pinal County part is split among Florence, J. O. Combs and Apache Junction, so ask the district to confirm.
